claims.claim: Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same. (Hook, A4: what a viewer who leaves at second two takes away.)
claims.note: Results: 'Such an inverse relation implies that a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; 'cellular biomass is overall approximately evenly spread among cell-size classes'; Conclusion: 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class'. The binning begins 'at red blood cells (4 x 10-11 g)', so 'from red blood cells up' is exact. 'Roughly' is load-bearing: in Fig. 4B (male, linear axis) the 26 classes run from about 0.05 to 7 kg, and the paper itself says variation lies 'within two orders of magnitude' outside the fat-muscle gap; the paper uses the same 'roughly'. 'Your body' generalises from the reference models, but the paper reports 'very similar patterns' for female and child (Fig. 3 caption). At second two the viewer has heard only the set-up ('Sort the cells in your body by...'), so nothing false is left behind; the full hook matches the paper's headline finding.

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study combined over fifteen hundred published sources to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.note: PNAS 120(39) e2303077120, published online 18 Sep 2023. Abstract: 'data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods: 'more than 1,500 published sources for 400 known cell types across 60 tissue systems ... giving 1,264 cell groups'. 'Estimate' matches 'we estimate total body counts'. Sorting by size: the whole-body size histogram of Fig. 3.

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.note: 'Our size distribution does not include these small cells [platelets, haploid sperm], and only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10-11 g)'; Methods: bins begin 'at the lower bound of erythrocytes'; 'We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes (blood platelets and the smallest haploid gamete cells)'. 'Sorted' correctly limits the claim to the binned set; red blood cells are not the smallest human cells overall.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.note: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; 'cell sizes vary over an enormous seven orders of magnitude from red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers'. The paper's 'size' is cell mass in grams, so 'heavier' is the right reading.

claims.claim: Now put those cells into size classes, where each class holds cells twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.note: Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 from small to large (octave size classes), beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.note: Fitted slope -0.97, 95% CI -1.09 to -0.87. Per doubling: 2^-0.97 = 0.51 (CI 0.47 to 0.55), i.e. about half. 'On average' is right: Fig. 3 bins scatter around the line (e.g. near 1e-5 g they fall well below it).

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.note: 'A slope near -1 implies a roughly inverse relation between cell size and count, such that an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'. 'Cancel out' = the paper's 'offset'; the next line's 'roughly' carries the approximation (slope -0.97, not exactly -1).

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.note: As claim 1. 'Every' is immediately qualified by the next spoken line ('With one exception: a dip'), which is how the paper frames it: 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude'.

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.note: 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10-6 g) and myocytes (near 10-4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass'. Fig. 4B male: three classes around 1e-5 g at about 0.3, 0.05 and 0.15 kg, against about 1 kg for a typical class. The paper names this gap as the one exception; the other irregularities it counts within the 'two orders of magnitude'.

claims.claim: In a typical woman the dip is smaller, and in a typical ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child (Fig. 4B ...)'. Fig. 4B agrees. 'Typical' stands for the paper's reference models, which its Significance calls 'a representative male, female, and 10-y-old child'; female and child are scaled from the male model, so 'typical' is as far as the wording can go.

claims.claim: Take a typical man. His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption (reference male): skeletal myocytes 'make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count'. 0.002% = 2e-5 = 1 in 50,000, and '<' matches 'fewer than'. Muscle fibres = skeletal myocytes.

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass in the body'; remainder given as 23.5 kg, so myocytes about 21.5 kg (48%).

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: '45 kg of cell biomass' (reference male). Cross-check: the 26 male class values read off Fig. 4B sum to about 44.6 kg.

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: cell biomass 'excludes noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'. Reference male is 70 kg (Approach, Methods); 45 + 25 = 70. 'Between them' = extracellular.

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3732 via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8580314/fullTextXML; Fig. 2 image (sciadv.abh3732-f2.jpg) from .../PMC8580314/supplementaryFiles; PNAS paper ref. 44
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne (Gt) wet weight (10^15 g), but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value'. The reconstruction is 'a "pristine" state, before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'; today 'the upper one-third of the biomass spectrum has been severely truncated', so the past tense and 'before industrial fishing' are needed and present. 'Most' matches 'most'. 'Too': the PNAS paper cites this ocean spectrum (ref. 44) as the same size distribution. Ocean classes are tenfold, not twofold; the line does not claim the same width.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120 via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML; literature search for later work (Firecrawl research index, 2023-10 to 2026), which surfaced doi:10.1016/j.biosystems.2024.105190 (abstract only)
claims.note: Discussion: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'; Conclusion: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'. 'No accepted process' = 'no universally recognized process'; the paper offers candidate mechanisms, which the wording allows. A 2024 Biosystems paper (Han, Bai & Wang) proposes a cell-division model for power-law scaling; that is a further proposal, not an accepted explanation, so 'yet' still holds as far as could be found.

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at almost every size.
claims.note: ≈36 trillion cells in the male, ≈29 trillion of them nonnucleated blood cells; myocytes <0.002% of nucleated cells. 'Almost every size' leaves room for the gap (claim 9); 'roughly' as in claim 1.

claims.claim: ROUGHLY THE SAME (first and last keyword cards)
claims.note: Shown with the hook and the closing line; as claims 1 and 17. The card keeps the qualifier 'roughly'.

claims.claim: 1,500+ SOURCES
claims.note: '>1,500 published sources' (Abstract); 'more than 1,500 published sources' (Methods).

claims.claim: RED BLOOD CELLS
claims.note: As claim 3: the binned distribution starts at red blood cells.
'more than a million-fold larger' in cell mass; seven orders of magnitude overall. '>' matches 'more than'.

claims.claim: ×2 CELL SIZE
claims.note: Octave classes, factor of 2 in cell mass (Methods).

claims.claim: HALF AS MANY
claims.note: As claim 6: slope -0.97 gives 0.51 per doubling. Shown while 'on average, about half' is spoken.

claims.claim: THEY CANCEL OUT
claims.note: As claim 7 ('offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor').

claims.claim: ABOUT THE SAME
claims.note: As claim 8; 'about' keeps the approximation.

claims.claim: ONE DIP
claims.note: As claim 9: the paper names one gap as the exception.

claims.claim: TYPICAL WOMAN
claims.note: Label only; refers to the 60 kg reference female ('representative'), as claim 10.

claims.claim: A TYPICAL MAN, sub 70 KG (154 LB)
claims.note: Reference male 70 kg (Approach; Methods: '70 kg, 176 cm'). 70 kg x 2.20462 = 154.3 lb, rounds to 154.
'<0.002% of the nucleated cell count' = fewer than 1 in 50,000 (claim 11).

claims.claim: ABOUT HALF
claims.note: 'about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass' (claim 12).

claims.claim: 45 KG, sub 99 LB
claims.note: 45 kg cell biomass (claim 13). 45 x 2.20462 = 99.2 lb, rounds to 99.

claims.claim: NOT CELLS, sub 25 KG (55 LB)
claims.note: '~25 kg' noncellular (Fig. 2 caption). 25 x 2.20462 = 55.1 lb, rounds to 55.

claims.note: 'extracellular water, protein, and minerals' (Fig. 2 caption).

claims.claim: THE OCEAN TOO
claims.note: As claim 15; shown with the spoken past-tense, pre-industrial qualifier, and the ocean chart is titled 'BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING'.

claims.claim: NOBODY KNOWS WHY
claims.note: As claim 16: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'.

claims.claim: NOT YET EXPLAINED
claims.note: As claim 16: 'no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'.

claims.claim: Axis 'CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE' from 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻² g; 26 size classes, each twice the mass of the one before, the first starting at 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120 via https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML; Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 images
claims.note: Methods: factor-of-2 bins 'beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'; red blood cells '4 x 10-11 g'. 4e-11 x 2^26 = 2.7e-3 g, inside the 1e-2 g end of the axis. Fig. 3 and Fig. 4B both show 26 binned points from about 5e-11 to 2e-3 g. Size is cell mass in g, as in the paper.

claims.claim: Axis marks 'RED BLOOD CELLS / FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g', 'FAT CELLS / ~10⁻⁶ g', 'MUSCLE FIBRES / ~10⁻⁴ g'
claims.note: 'red blood cells (4 x 10-11 g)', 'adipocytes (near 10-6 g) and myocytes (near 10-4 g)'. 'FROM' correctly marks 4e-11 g as the lower bound, not a typical red-cell mass. In Fig. 4B (male) the fat peak sits at about 1e-6 g and the muscle peak at about 2-3e-4 g; '~10^-4 g' is the paper's own 'near 10^-4 g'.

claims.claim: Bars 'NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': a falling staircase, with a dip between the fat and muscle marks
claims.note: Fig. 3: binned counts fall from about 1e13 to about 1e5 along a slope of -0.97. Between the fat and muscle classes the binned counts drop below the fitted line (near 1e-5 g about 1.5e6 against roughly 5e7 on the line, more than tenfold), then rejoin it at the myocyte classes, so a dip in the count staircase is what the data show. Labelled 'SCHEMATIC' on screen (A6).

claims.claim: Bars 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': roughly level, a dip between the fat and muscle marks, a raised peak at the fat mark and at the muscle mark, the muscle peak taller
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120; Fig. 4 image (pnas.2303077120fig04.jpg), male panel of 4B enlarged and read class by class
claims.note: Male classes read off Fig. 4B: mostly 0.4-2 kg; fat peak about 3.7 kg near 1e-6 g; dip about 0.3, 0.05, 0.15 kg near 1e-5 g; muscle peak about 7.0 and 6.3 kg near 2-5e-4 g. So level-with-two-peaks-and-a-dip, with the muscle peak taller, matches the reference man (in the female panel the fat peak is the taller, so the chart must stay labelled as the man; it is). Simplification noted, not a misstatement: the schematic leaves out a smaller bump in the red-blood-cell class (about 2.5 kg) and the tapering end classes; the paper itself singles out only the adipocyte and myocyte peaks and the gap, and the bars say 'SCHEMATIC' (A6).

claims.claim: Text card 'THE DIP BETWEEN FAT AND MUSCLE': 'TYPICAL MAN: MOST PROMINENT', 'TYPICAL WOMAN: SMALLER', 'TYPICAL 10-YEAR-OLD: FAINTER STILL'
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child'. Of the three, the male gap is therefore the most prominent; Fig. 4B agrees (male trough about 0.05 kg between 3.7 and 7 kg peaks; female and child troughs shallower relative to their peaks). Text only, so no linear-vs-log distortion.

claims.claim: Grid of 250 × 200 dots captioned '50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · AT MOST 1 MUSCLE FIBRE', one dot ringed
claims.note: 250 x 200 = 50,000. Skeletal myocytes '<0.002% of the nucleated cell count' = under 1 in 50,000, so 'AT MOST 1' per 50,000 is correct and does not overstate.

claims.claim: Bar 'ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG' half filled 'MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF'; extended by 'NOT CELLS · 25 KG' to '70 KG MAN', 'WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS'; lengths drawn 45:25
claims.note: 45 kg cell biomass with skeletal myocytes 'about half' (Fig. 1 caption); '~25 kg' extracellular water, protein and minerals (Fig. 2 caption); 45 + 25 = 70 kg reference male. Drawn to scale.

claims.claim: Ocean card: axis 'SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE', level bars titled 'BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC', first three bars higher, last two lower
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3732; Fig. 2 image (sciadv.abh3732-f2.jpg) from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8580314/supplementaryFiles, panel A enlarged
claims.note: Fig. 2A (pristine, upper 200 m, tenfold body-mass classes): first three classes about 2.5, 2.5 and 1.9 Gt; most others about 0.6-1 Gt ('all other groups sum to approximately 1 Gt'); the last two (marine mammals, red) about 0.12 and 0.06 Gt. Matches 'bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below'. The two fish classes just before the mammals (about 0.5 Gt) are drawn level, which the paper's 'approximately 1 Gt' covers; labelled 'SCHEMATIC'. The paper's x axis is body mass, so 'size' as mass is consistent; 'pre-1850' = 'before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals'.
